story: Personal Azure learning experience; not a commercial or agent demonstration
mode: Eight static annotated slides built from actual screenshots. Not live gameplay footage. No model invocation or public score submission.

segments.narration: When I first started learning Azure, I mainly used Microsoft Learn and the documentation. They gave me useful concepts. But as a beginner, I found it harder to connect those concepts together.

segments.narration: I understood App Service, SQL, and caching on their own. But when traffic increased, what should I change? Would more App instances help, or was the database the problem? Those connections were less clear to me.
segments.title:
I knew what the services were.
I didn't know how they behaved together.

segments.narration: So I built this. Stack and Survive is a small game where beginners can experience a few Azure architecture decisions, rather than just read their definitions.
segments.title: So I built this.
segments.visibleText:
So I built this.

A simple game for experiencing Azure architecture decisions.

segments.narration: Traffic comes in, and you change the architecture. You can add capacity, introduce cache, or protect the edge. The game then shows what happens to availability, lost sales, and running cost.
segments.title:
You make a change.
The system reacts.
segments.visibleText:

segments.narration: This is the part I care about. What would you change? More App instances? A stronger database? It isn't about clicking Scale Out. It's about noticing which layer is under pressure, and why.
segments.title: What would you change?
segments.visibleText:
What would you change?

More App instances?

Scale the database?

Add cache?

Protect the edge?

The interesting part isn't clicking Scale Out.
It's deciding which layer is actually under pressure.

segments.narration: This run survived. But was it a good architecture? Maybe I added more capacity than I needed. Keeping the service available matters, but so does the cost of the choices I made.
segments.title: It survived.
segments.visibleText:
It survived.

But was it a good
architecture?

Did I build too much?
What did it cost?

Availability is only part of the story.

segments.narration: After the run, I want people to look back and try another choice. They can return to Microsoft Learn with a more concrete question. The idea is to play, observe, reflect, and try again.
segments.title: What would you change next time?
segments.visibleText:
What would you change next time?

Look back at the run.

Try a different choice.

Return to Microsoft Learn
with a more concrete question.

play → observe
reflect → try again

segments.narration: This is not a replacement for Microsoft Learn. I hope it gives customers a simpler, more enjoyable first step into Azure, and helps them feel more comfortable exploring the real services afterward.
segments.title:
Making the first step
into Azure easier.
segments.visibleText:

Not a replacement for Microsoft Learn.
Just another way to get started.
